title: EXPLORE A PRODUCT YOU MAKE YOURSELF WITH CHATGPT
content:
Making a product yourself gives you direct control over how it is produced, but it also makes your production time and capacity part of the business model.

Before worrying about logos or sales channels, it is useful to understand what you can make consistently, what each unit requires, and how much production the business could realistically support.

YOUR LABOR IS PART OF THE UNIT COST
If an item takes two hours to make, selling ten more requires roughly twenty more production hours unless the process changes. That does not make handmade products a bad model. It means capacity deserves attention early.

QUESTIONS BEYOND CAN I MAKE IT?
Can you make it consistently? Source materials reliably? Store and ship it safely? What happens when an order is damaged? How many units can you make in a normal week without turning work you enjoy into a workload you hate?

For regulated or safety-sensitive categories, use the interview to identify questions, then qualified sources to answer them.

SIMPLE CAPACITY EXAMPLE
If a product takes 45 minutes of hands-on work and you can devote 15 production hours each week, the theoretical maximum is 20 units before setup, cleanup, packing, mistakes, customer service, and everything else.

That does not tell you whether the business works. It shows why production time belongs in the questions from the beginning.

WHAT PRODUCTION CAPACITY MEANS

Suppose you make candles yourself and one candle takes about 20 minutes of hands-on work across the steps that require your attention.

Selling three is not a capacity problem. Selling 300 might be.

Capacity is simply how much work your current process can realistically produce in the available time, space, and equipment. As orders increase, you may discover that a particular step, such as pouring, curing, assembly, packaging, or personalization, limits how many finished products can leave the business.

That limiting step is often called a bottleneck.

WHY UNIT ECONOMICS MATTER

If a candle sells for $25, that does not mean you made $25.

The wax, fragrance, vessel, wick, label, packaging, payment fees, marketplace fees, damaged units, shipping contribution, and other relevant costs can reduce what remains. Your own production time matters too, even when no one sends you an invoice for it.

"Unit economics" is simply a way of asking what happens financially when you sell one more unit.

You do not need perfect accounting at the idea stage. You do need to avoid evaluating a handmade product using the retail price alone.

WHAT A USEFUL CHATGPT EXPLORATION SHOULD LEAVE YOU WITH

By the end, you should be able to describe:

What you would make.

Who it is for.

Why they would choose it.

What materials, equipment, skills, space, and time the current version appears to require.

Which step is likely to limit production.

What one unit appears to require before broader business expenses.

What product-specific safety, labeling, legal, insurance, shipping, or other requirements need independent research.

And what you would test before investing heavily.

That is enough to turn "maybe I could sell things I make" into a product direction you can investigate.

HOW TO USE THIS
Use the prompt below to turn this branch into your version of the business. Answer the questions honestly, ask for clarification when you need it, and do not treat external facts as verified just because ChatGPT mentions them.

WHAT THIS INTERVIEW SHOULD PRODUCE

By the end, you should have one handmade or self-produced physical product direction, a rough production picture, the likely capacity bottleneck, and a list of product-specific questions that require real research.

ChatGPT should use your actual skills, tools, space, time, and interests rather than assuming handmade means crafts.

It should not certify safety, legal compliance, labeling, insurance needs, or production economics.

COPY & PASTE INTO CHATGPT

During the interview:
- Ask one question at a time unless a small group of tightly related questions is genuinely easier to answer together.
- Use my answers before deciding what to ask next. Do not run through a generic questionnaire when an answer makes a question irrelevant.
- If I say "I don't know," help me identify what I need to decide or research. Do not silently invent an answer for me.
- Explain unfamiliar business terms in plain language when they first become relevant.
- Separate assumptions from facts that require outside verification.
- Do not turn this into a marketing or customer-acquisition plan unless the purpose of this specific interview requires it.
- When you have enough information, stop interviewing me and give me the requested conclusion, including the important unknowns and next research questions.
Ask me one question at a time unless a small group of closely related questions would be easier to answer together. If I say I don't know, help me identify what I would need to decide or research instead of inventing an answer for me.

Interview me about a physical product I could make myself. Ask what I can make or want to learn to make, my existing skills and equipment, who the product would be for, materials, time per unit, production capacity, consistency, quality, packaging, storage, and shipping considerations.

Help me identify the cost and capacity questions I need to calculate. If the category raises safety, labeling, licensing, insurance, or regulatory issues, flag those for independent verification rather than guessing.

End with a specific self-made product direction and a short list of the most important feasibility questions.

NEXT → PDF 46 if clear; PDF 14 if manufacturer production sounds better; PDF 12 to reconsider.

While interviewing me, follow these rules:

Treat production capacity as part of the idea rather than a problem to solve later. If the user describes a labor-intensive product, ask enough about time per unit and available production time to expose obvious capacity conflicts.

Do not assume handmade means small, premium, inexpensive to start, or easy to sell. Those depend on the actual product and customer.

If safety or regulation may matter, identify the category of question without pretending to give approval.

At the end, give me:
- Product
- Intended customer/use
- Production method
- Approximate capacity questions
- Materials/equipment questions
- Operational constraints
- Verification needs
- Specific business-direction statement
